question: How could storing electricity for days to weeks become ten times cheaper than today, so that wind and solar can run a whole grid through long calm, dark spells? Propose fundamentally new mechanisms or system designs - not incremental improvements of existing battery chemistries.

readings.label: Cheaper hardware per delivered kWh
readings.goal: A storage device whose total cost (energy store plus charge and discharge conversion plus round-trip losses) per kWh actually delivered over a few cycles a year is ten times lower than today's.
readings.crux: The answers make the bulk medium nearly free (ore heaps, salt ponds, iron piles, quicklime, gas fields) but assume the power-conversion side (membrane and electrochemical stacks, reversible SOCs, iron combustors, CO2 turbines) is cheap and efficient, when at a handful of cycles a year that converter capex and 30-60% round-trip loss dominate the cost.

readings.label: Firm grid through dunkelflaute economics
readings.goal: A system and market design where keeping a wind and solar grid reliable through rare multi-week lulls costs ten times less, whether by storage, flexible demand or some mix.
readings.crux: The answers rely on assets that sit idle or under-used most years (overbuilt factories, stacks used once a season) and wave at "contracts" or "markets" to pay for them, without solving who funds and guarantees capacity whose value shows up only in rare, uncertain extreme events.

readings.label: Bulk media that really deliver power
readings.goal: A physical mechanism where cheap, abundant bulk material at TWh scale can be charged and discharged at grid power rates reliably after weeks or months of idling.
readings.crux: The answers assume cheap bulk stores can be accessed fast enough and stay usable, leaving unsolved the transport and kinetics limits (reaction fronts moving through ore heaps, membrane fouling with raw brine, sintering of solids over many cycles, reservoir gas mixing) that decide whether cheap tonnes turn into usable megawatts.

crux: The answers make the bulk medium nearly free (ore heaps, salt ponds, iron piles, quicklime, gas fields) but assume the power-conversion side (membrane and electrochemical stacks, reversible SOCs, iron combustors, CO2 turbines) is cheap and efficient, when at a handful of cycles a year that converter capex and 30-60% round-trip loss dominate the cost.

laws.law: Transport-length law for any bulk or in-situ electrode bed, pit, pond, layer or current collector discharged over time t: the usable thickness is L = √(2κΔV·t/q_vol) for ion conduction, L = √(D·t) or √(nFDc/j) for diffusion, and the collector width is W = √(8ΔV/(i·R_s)). Areal energy is therefore capped at E_area ≈ √(2κ·ΔV·V·t·e_vol). Slab, pond, ore-body or bed size cancels out, and conductivity × time controls instead (E05, E07, E08, E13, E14, E17, E18, E20, E21).
laws.out: metre-thick beds, deep pits, ore lenses or waste ponds wired with sparse electrodes. It also rules out pond-wide planar collectors and anything relying on low-conductivity pore water (about 0.01-0.1 S/m).
laws.opens: thin cm-scale layers with high-κ electrolyte (KOH at about 12 S/m) or a conductive filler (coke). Long discharge helps because L grows as √t, which allows multi-day electrodes about 50x thicker and so about 50x less foil, separator and can per kWh. Advection escapes the law entirely: a Darcy flow delivers nFcu/2 per area whatever the bed length, at about 0.1% pumping power.

laws.law: Crossover-ohmic invariant for any two-species cell kept apart by a diffusive barrier (separator, sand, spent buffer layer or porous divider): (crossover fraction) × (ohmic fraction) = nF·D_active·c/(σ·V). Barrier thickness, current density and even temperature cancel, since by Walden's rule D and σ both scale as 1/viscosity. Lowering the current (oversizing) makes crossover worse (E12, E19, E20, E22).
laws.out: small, concentrated (about 1 M) redox ions behind thin porous separators. It also rules out fixing leakage with thicker barriers, heating, or slower, oversized cells.
laws.opens: a large ratio of salt mobility to active-species mobility. That means macromolecular or redox-polymer actives (D about 1e-13), or dilute actives (about 0.2 M) in strong supporting salt (about 4 M NaCl). Longer discharge also helps, because it lowers the leak per stored charge.

laws.law: Homogeneous co-mixing law for any membrane-free or single-phase design where the charged species meet in the bulk: the loss rate k·c² (diffusion-limited, k about 1e8-1e10 M⁻¹s⁻¹) beats the useful rate j/(nF·h) by about 10^10-10^11. A surface catalyst cannot gate a bulk reaction, and metastable charged states that live nanoseconds cannot reach electrodes seconds away (E10, E22, E23).
laws.out: mixed membrane-free channels, strain-energy or metastable-molecule cells, and designs that rely on a slow bulk reaction.
laws.opens: spatial separation with a spent-electrolyte buffer of thickness s, where the leak falls as exp(−s²/4Dt). Short contact times (minutes) with s ≫ √(Dt), for example a 1.5 mm spent lamina, cut the leak to about 1%.

laws.law: Converter-hours law for any long-duration store covering a lull of length T: it delivers min(P·T, E), so it needs E/P ≤ T. Power-side cost per kWh is c_P/(E/P), only about $0.5-1/kWh at E/P of 170-340 h. Forecast lead time and shared inverters barely matter, so the storage medium sets the cost (E04, E17).
laws.out: very cheap undersized converters slowly trickling a giant store (E/P ≫ T). It also rules out expecting savings from early discharge, forecasting or shared grid ties.
laws.opens: E/P ≈ T/2 (about 250 h) with the converter running about 50% of hours. All of the 10x cost cut must then come from $/kWh of the medium (about ≤$20/kWh).

laws.law: Host-flow law for any design that piggybacks on existing infrastructure or by-product streams (pipes, a chemical market, mine drainage, waste liquor): energy or power = host volume or throughput × concentration of the active species. It scales with the host, not with the grid (E01, E02, E06).
laws.out: dilute or small hosts, such as water mains (about 100x short), the world H2O2 market (about 0.45 GW against 10 GW per grid) and acid-mine drainage (about 11 years per GWh).
laws.opens: concentrated streams. Pickle liquor at about 120 g/L Fe is 600x richer, about 1 GWh/yr per line. Use the host only for cheap medium and size the power stage to the grid.

laws.law: Stress-holding bound for any store that keeps energy as load in a structure (pressed clay, hydraulic, elastic or overburden): energy per mass of structure ≤ f·σ/(1.5ρ), about 1-3 Wh/kg for steel, whatever the pressure, plate or column size. Cost is therefore (structure $/kg)/(Wh/kg) (E09, E16).
laws.out: any design whose stored state needs continuous load-bearing containment (hundreds of kg of steel per kWh). Earth overburden cannot carry pressures above about 10 km of rock either.
laws.opens: latched or force-free stored states, such as strain-crystallised locked rubber that carries no force. Housing then drops to bale-yard cost, and cost is set only by the medium's $/kg ÷ Wh/kg.

laws.law: Frozen-mobility law for any design that locks charge by freezing or vitrifying the electrolyte: by Walden's rule, conductivity ∝ 1/viscosity, so the same immobility that stops self-discharge also cuts conductance by about 10^6. Thawing costs c_p·ΔT, about 1.6x the stored energy density (E11).
laws.out: glass-locked or solid-locked electrolytes discharged without heat recovery, or at normal current densities and gaps.
laws.opens: ≥90% heat recuperation, with large, thin-gap, low-current stacks that are affordable only because discharge lasts about 100 h or more.

laws.law: Wetted-surface self-discharge law for any porous metal or iron electrode held for weeks: pores with capillary entry pressure 2γ/r above the drainage head (r of about µm, about 1.4 bar against about 0.1 bar) stay flooded. Self-discharge is therefore set by the hydrogen overpotential on the wetted surface, not by liquid level (E03).
laws.out: drain-to-hold or dry-storage schemes for porous electrodes, which still lose about 1%/day.
laws.opens: cheap kinetic poisons for hydrogen evolution, such as about 1 wt% Bi₂S₃ at about $0.3/kWh, giving 0.1-0.2%/day loss.
